items.title: 5.4.4 Influence of hydrogen bonding on the properties of water

source_refs.note: Topic 5.4.4, printed pages 102-103 (Figures 5.6 and 5.7), with Quick Check 5.4 (d to f) as the self-check.

blocks.text: Structure and low density of ice

Water molecules have a tetrahedral structure, with the two lone pairs of oxygen at two corners of the tetrahedron. When water is cooled and ice forms, the molecules become more regular and this regularity extends through the whole structure; empty spaces are created in the extensively hydrogen-bonded structure. This is why water occupies 9 per cent more space when it freezes and its density decreases, so ice floats. Because of this so-called anomalous behaviour of ice, fish and other living creatures survive under frozen lakes and oceans: the ice blanket covers the surface because of its low density and insulates the water beneath from the environment. Part of a glacier floats for the same reason.
Water has a high specific heat capacity because of its unique molecular structure, which allows strong hydrogen bonds.
Anomalous heat of vaporization and boiling point

The enthalpy change of vaporization of the group 16 hydrides rises regularly from H2S to H2Po, because these molecules are bound by weak London dispersion forces that become stronger with increasing atomic size down the group from S to Po. If water followed this trend its heat of vaporization would be the lowest in the group; instead water has the highest enthalpy change of vaporization, 41 kJ per mol, because it is exceptionally hydrogen bonded, which makes it difficult to break the forces among its molecules and vaporize it. The boiling point of water is also remarkably higher than that of the other group 16 hydrides: the energy needed to pull water molecules apart is very high, so high temperatures are needed to boil it.

The surface tension and viscosity of water are also very high. Surface tension is a downward pull on the molecules at the surface, making the surface stretched and strained; the pull comes from the attraction of the inner molecules through hydrogen bonds. Viscosity is a liquid's resistance to flow; water is more viscous than many liquids, including the lower hydrocarbons and alcohols such as hexane and ethanol, again because of its strong hydrogen bonds. Alcohols can form hydrogen bonds, but far fewer and weaker than water; hydrocarbons cannot form them at all.

Right: a graph of boiling point or heat of vaporization against the hydrides H2O to H2Po, a blue line rising steadily from H2S, a grey dashed extension showing where water would fall, and a red point for water far above.
blocks.caption: The open structure of ice and water's anomalous boiling point and heat of vaporization among the group 16 hydrides (original diagram after Figures 5.6 and 5.7; heights schematic).
blocks.long_description: In ice each oxygen is hydrogen bonded to its neighbours in a regular tetrahedral network full of empty space, so ice is less dense than water and floats, insulating the water below. Down group 16 the hydrides boil at steadily higher temperatures as their London forces grow with size; water should be lowest but is by far the highest, boiling at 100 degrees C with a heat of vaporization of 41 kJ per mol, because its hydrogen bonds must be broken first. The same bonds raise its heat capacity, surface tension and viscosity.

blocks.prompt: The boiling point differences between CH3CH3 (-89 degrees C) and CH3OH (65 degrees C) and between butane (0 degrees C) and propanol (97 degrees C) are 154 and 97 degrees. Explain why the difference shrinks as the molecules grow, and why acetic acid forms dimers when pure but not in water.
blocks.explanation: The alcohol's extra boiling point comes from its hydrogen bonds, which add roughly the same amount in each pair, while the London forces of the hydrocarbon chain grow with its length. In the larger pair the chain's London forces are a bigger share of the total attraction, so the hydrogen bond makes a smaller relative difference. Pure acetic acid molecules pair up through two hydrogen bonds between their COOH groups; in water the acid's O-H and C=O groups hydrogen bond to the many surrounding water molecules instead, so the dimers break up.

items: Ice: a regular hydrogen-bonded network with empty spaces, 9 per cent more volume, lower density, floats and insulates the water beneath; water also has a high specific heat capacity.

Water's heat of vaporization (41 kJ per mol) and boiling point are far above the group 16 trend, and its surface tension and viscosity are high, all because of extensive hydrogen bonding (alcohols less, hydrocarbons none).
